newsitem.title: USA: Processing is Fidelity's next growth area-Johnson.
newsitem.headline: Processing is Fidelity's next growth area-Johnson.

text.p: The head of Fidelity Investments said late on Thursday he saw the next area of growth for the largest U.S. mutual fund company will be in doing processing work for its corporate customers.

"I expect the next billion (dollar) milestone will come from a rise in processing services that are closely related to our investment services," Fidelity chairman and chief executive officer Edward Johnson III said at a public lecture in Boston's Faneuil Hall.

"By that I mean putting together in one system all the financial rewards functions -- payroll, retirement benefits, medical benefits and human resource reporting," said Johnson, who heads the mutual fund company with $450 billion in assets.
"This is already today in America a multibillion-dollar market and I believe a great place for our next expansion. It is a business very close to our own business," he said.

Fidelity has experienced tremendous growth partly because it handles a lion's share of the 401K pension plans, in which employees contribute a specific sum regularly on a tax-deferred basis, offered by corporate America.
In September, a Fidelity spokeswoman said an estimated $1 billion will flow into its domestic equity funds and another $1 billion will find its way into the money market accounts.
Cash into Fidelity's international equity funds remained flat, she said.

A change in portfolio managers at Magellan, the company's largest mutual fund, caused outflows from that fund which now stands at $50 billion, down from its high of $54 billion. The spokeswoman said Magellan redemptions "have slowed significantly."

Critics have wondered if Magellan in particular and Fidelity in general has grown so large that it has become unwieldy. Johnson said $450 billion in assets "seems like a pretty big number" but the total stock investment in Fidelity funds are less than 3.0 percent of the value of U.S. stocks.
"Internationally...we own only 1.0 percent of stocks worldwide. In my mind, that leaves plenty of room for growth," he said.

Size has its advantages. For the first seven years, Fidelity's money fund, discount brokerage and insurance businesses all lost money for their first seven years, but being large allowed Fidelity "financial stability," Johnson said.
"That means more cash flow to do what's right for institutions...allows us to continuously develop systems which can take two to four years to complete...and be successful."
He noted advertising used to form 8.0 to 9.0 percent of Fidelity's gross revenues, but now because of the company's size, advertising represents 3.0 percent.
Of course there are downsides to being so large. Johnson, who has used technology to grow Fidelity, estimated the company's capital expenditures "will run $700 million to $800 million this year."

"Growth is a natural by-product of doing a good job for our shareholders... Size is not an issue. Doing an excellent job is," he said, and warned that large companies must continually guard against the risks of becoming "fat, dumb and lazy."

"One of the ways we guard against (these risks) is the Japanese practice of kaizen...(which) means, no matter what you do or how long you've been doing it, part of your job is figuring out how to do your work better tommorrow than you did today," Johnson said.
